identity.title: Emergence in non-neural models: grokking modular arithmetic via average gradient outer product

problem.claim: Explain grokking in modular-arithmetic learning and determine whether it depends on neural architectures or gradient-descent optimization.

gap.claim: The abstract challenges the framing of grokking as specific to neural networks or gradient descent, and examines feature learning as an alternative explanation.

contributions.claim: Applies Recursive Feature Machines with AGOP to modular arithmetic using general machine-learning models.
Reports grokking-like transitions in kernel machines and block-circulant feature learning in both RFM and neural networks.
Links RFM’s learned block-circulant features to the Fourier Multiplication Algorithm.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors state that emergence can arise purely from learning task-relevant features, rather than being specific to neural architectures or gradient-descent methods.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that iterated RFM with kernel machines transitions rapidly from near-zero random test accuracy to perfect test accuracy.
They report that training loss stays identically zero and test loss remains constant during initial iterations, so these losses do not predict the transition.
They report that RFM gradually learns block-circulant features, while neural networks solving the same tasks learn analogous features.

narrative_sequence.summary: Grokking is introduced as delayed test-accuracy improvement after perfect training accuracy, often viewed as emergence.
The work tests whether grokking requires neural networks or gradient descent by using RFM for modular arithmetic.
With kernel machines, RFM produces a rapid shift from near-zero to perfect test accuracy despite uninformative early losses.
The transition is attributed to gradual learning of block-circulant features; neural networks learn corresponding features.
The abstract presents evidence connecting these features to Fourier multiplication and AGOP-mediated feature learning.

source_observation.claim: The abstract contrasts an abrupt accuracy transition with losses that provide no predictive signal, then identifies gradual feature learning as the determining process.

lessons.interpretation: When outcome metrics look discontinuous, tracking internal representations may reveal the gradual mechanism behind the change.
lessons.application: Pair performance curves with measurements of task-relevant feature structure and test whether representation changes precede the transition.
lessons.exception: This is unsuitable when representations are unavailable or when the task has no meaningful feature-level diagnostic.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify datasets, model sizes, optimization details, transition timing, or quantitative comparisons beyond the stated accuracy outcomes.
The theoretical evidence for implementing Fourier multiplication is not detailed enough here to assess its formal scope or proof status.
